19.text: MLX is the Apple-Silicon branch of the same transformer story: familiar tensor code, but with unified memory and lazy execution changing the runtime model underneath.

20.text: Same dataset, so the new thing to notice is MLX's execution model rather than a different workload.

21.text: The outer loop stays simple. The interesting differences arrive from how MLX represents arrays and when it actually executes work.

24.text: mlx.core looks simple on the surface, but unified memory is the key idea: CPU and GPU see the same physical RAM, so data movement looks very different from PyTorch or JAX.

25.text: The layer API feels comfortably familiar, which helps isolate what MLX changes at the runtime and memory level.

26.text: Compared with JAX, MLX swings back toward convenience. The interesting question becomes how much simplicity you get while still taking advantage of Apple hardware.

27.text: MLX still stores parameters in trees, so some of the explicitness from JAX remains even though the code reads more like a high-level framework.

29.text: Keep the experiment stable so differences in behavior can be traced back to MLX itself.

30.text: MLX has its own RNG, seeded separately.

35.text: Dataset path, shared across all labs.

36.text: If the names dataset is not already on disk, download it automatically so the tutorial is self-contained.

39.text: URL pointing to the raw names dataset hosted in Karpathy's repository.

42.text: Read the text file and split it into individual name strings. Each line becomes one training document.

43.text: Randomize the training order so the model does not memorize sequences of names.

46.text: The set of unique characters across all names forms our vocabulary. Each character gets a fixed integer ID.

47.text: The beginning-of-sequence token doubles as the end-of-sequence marker for name boundaries.

48.text: The vocabulary has 27 tokens: 26 lowercase letters plus the BOS/EOS marker.

55.text: Split attention into 4 parallel heads so each can focus on different character relationships.

56.text: A single transformer layer keeps things minimal. One layer is enough to learn meaningful character-level patterns for names.

57.text: Names up to 16 characters fit in the context window. Most names are well within this limit.

58.text: Each attention head works with 4 dimensions, matching the small model scale.

61.text: RMSNorm module. MLX uses __call__ instead of PyTorch's forward, Python convention for callable objects.

64.text: A tiny constant added before division to prevent numerical explosion when activations are near zero. Standard in every norm layer.

66.text: MLX uses __call__ for the forward pass, not forward. A stylistic choice, both work.

67.text: Element-wise square, then mean. MLX arrays support the same operations as NumPy.

68.text: Scale by inverse RMS. mx.rsqrt is a fused reciprocal square root.

71.text: Self-attention module, structurally identical to PyTorch's version in lab 03.

74.text: nn.Linear in MLX works just like PyTorch's, stores a weight matrix, applies matrix multiply.

75.text: Project the normalized input into key vectors that other positions will compare against.

76.text: Project the input into value vectors that carry content to be aggregated by attention.

77.text: Project the concatenated multi-head output back into the embedding space.

79.text: Forward pass. No batch dimension here, MLX's single-example version operates on (T, C) tensors.

80.text: Extract the sequence length from the input tensor to set up attention masks.

81.text: Reshape into heads: (T, D) -> (T, nh, hd) -> (nh, T, hd). Same pattern across every lab.

82.text: Keys get the same multi-head reshape as queries. Each head's keys will be compared against only that head's queries.

83.text: Values get the same multi-head reshape. Each head independently retrieves content from its own subspace of the embedding.

85.text: Compute attention scores by taking the dot product of queries and keys, scaled by the square root of head dimension to prevent saturation.

86.text: Causal mask. MLX's triu works identically to NumPy/PyTorch.

87.text: Apply the causal mask by element-wise selection: future positions get a large negative score, so softmax leaves them almost no weight. Note -1e9 rather than -inf, which stays finite, so a row that somehow lost every key would come out uniform instead of NaN.

88.text: Turn raw attention scores into a probability distribution so weights sum to one.

90.text: Attention output: weighted sum, transpose back, reshape to (T, D).

91.text: Project the combined multi-head output through the final linear layer.

97.text: Expand the representation to 4x the embedding dimension. This wider hidden layer gives the MLP more capacity for nonlinear transformations.

98.text: Compress the expanded hidden state back to the original embedding dimension.

100.text: Run the input through the MLP sub-layer combining expansion, activation, and contraction.

101.text: ReLU spelled out as an element-wise maximum. mlx.nn.relu and nn.ReLU both exist and would work here; writing the maximum keeps the line next to lab 02, where this same clamp had to be differentiated by hand.

104.text: Transformer block, same norm-attend-add, norm-MLP-add pattern.

107.text: Normalize the input before passing it to the attention sub-layer for stable training.

108.text: The self-attention sub-layer that mixes information across positions in the sequence.

109.text: Normalize before the feed-forward network, following the pre-norm transformer pattern.

110.text: The feed-forward network that processes each position independently after attention mixing.

112.text: Forward: same two-line transformer block as PyTorch.

113.text: Apply attention with a residual connection: normalize, attend to other positions, and add the result back to the original signal.

114.text: Apply the MLP with a residual connection that preserves the original signal.

118.text: The complete GPT model combining embeddings, normalization, transformer layers, and output head.

121.text: The token embedding lookup table. Each of the 27 tokens maps to a learned 16-dimensional vector capturing what that character 'means' to the model.

122.text: The position embedding table. Each of the 16 positions maps to a learned vector that tells the model where a token sits in the sequence.

123.text: Normalize embeddings before entering the transformer stack. This initial normalization keeps activations stable from the very start.

124.text: Transformer layers. MLX uses a plain Python list (not ModuleList), the framework still discovers parameters through its tree-walking utilities.

125.text: The output head projects from 16-dim embedding space to 27-dim vocabulary logits. Each output score indicates how likely a character is to come next.

127.text: Run the full model on the current input to produce next-token predictions.

128.text: Extract the sequence length from the input to generate matching position indices.

129.text: Look up a learned embedding vector for each input token in the sequence.

130.text: Generate position indices [0, 1, ..., n-1] and look up their learned embeddings. These give the model a sense of token order.

131.text: Combine token and position embeddings and normalize before entering the transformer.

132.text: Pass the representation through each transformer layer in sequence. The code scales to any depth even though we use just one layer here.

133.text: Each layer transforms the hidden state.

134.text: Map from embedding space to vocabulary logits. Each output value is a raw score for how likely each of the 27 tokens is to come next.

140.text: Instantiate the model. No .to(device) needed, MLX's unified memory means arrays are already accessible by both CPU and GPU.

144.text: Re-initialize every weight to N(0, 0.08) so this lab starts where all the others do. nn.Module.apply maps a function over every parameter array in place, in MLX just as in PyTorch, and it is the idiomatic hook for re-initializing, casting or quantizing a whole model.

145.text: Sum up all parameter sizes to report the total number of trainable weights.

148.text: Adam hyperparameters, same across all labs.

151.text: The loss function takes the model as its first argument, which is how MLX's value_and_grad knows which parameters to differentiate.

152.text: Run the full model on the current input to get next-token prediction logits.

154.text: Manual log-softmax, logits - logsumexp(logits), which is more numerically stable than log(softmax(x)).

155.text: Get the number of tokens in the input for indexing into log probabilities.

156.text: Gather target log-probs and negate their mean, cross-entropy loss.

160.text: nn.value_and_grad creates a function that returns both the loss value and gradients in one call. MLX's equivalent of PyTorch's forward + backward.

161.text: MLX's built-in Adam optimizer. Unlike JAX where we wrote Adam manually, MLX provides a stateful optimizer like PyTorch.

174.text: The switch that makes the compiler claim testable. Set it to False, rerun, and compare the printed ms/step instead of taking the speedup on trust.

175.text: The parameters and the optimizer moments are read and written by the step but never passed as arguments, so they have to be declared to mx.compile explicitly. Compare JAX, where the same state has to be threaded through the signature by hand.

178.text: The step as an ordinary Python function: gradients, then update. Wrapping it afterwards means the uncompiled and compiled versions are literally the same code.

179.text: Compute loss and gradients in one call. Clean and efficient.

180.text: Push the computed gradients into the model's parameters via the optimizer. MLX's stateful optimizer applies the Adam update rule internally.

185.text: mx.compile is MLX's counterpart to jax.jit: trace once, then hand fused kernels to the device instead of dispatching operation by operation. Like jit, it specializes on input shapes, so a new sequence length costs another trace.

187.text: Train for 1000 steps, one document per step. Each iteration: forward, loss, gradients, Adam update.

188.text: Count the distinct sequence lengths, because each one is another trace. This is lab 05's shape-recompilation story in MLX form, and lab 06's fix of padding everything to one static width would work here unchanged.

189.text: Two buckets, first-time shapes and repeats, so the cost of tracing is separated from the cost of running.

191.text: Iterate over training steps, processing one name per step to update model weights.

192.text: Cycle through the dataset with modular indexing. After processing all names, loop back for another pass.

193.text: Convert the name into a sequence of integer token IDs with BOS markers at both ends.

194.text: Clip to the maximum context window. Most names fit easily, but this guard prevents overflow on unusually long entries.

196.text: Convert the Python token list to an MLX array so it can flow through the computation graph for forward and backward passes.

197.text: Wrap the target tokens as an MLX array. These are the correct next characters the model should learn to predict.

199.text: Ask before recording, so the step can be charged to the right bucket. Both paths run identical Python.

204.text: Linear learning-rate decay, the same schedule as every other lab. The learning rate lives in the optimizer state that the compiled step captured, so changing it here is picked up without forcing a retrace, which is exactly why it is an mx.array and not a Python float.

206.text: Start the clock around the step only, so the number is about the framework rather than about tokenizing a name in Python.

207.text: One call: forward pass, gradients, and the Adam update, compiled together.

213.text: MLX is lazy, so the update above is only a graph so far. loss_val.item() further down does force the loss, so this call is not what "gets the number". Its job is to bound the graph: without it the pending work would keep accumulating step after step until scheduling and memory dominate the run.

214.text: Elapsed milliseconds. On a first-time shape this includes the trace; afterwards it is the compiled kernels alone.

215.text: Sort the step into the right bucket in one expression. MLX traces far more cheaply than XLA, so the two averages below sit much closer together than lab 05's.

217.text: Print the loss periodically so we can monitor whether the model is learning.

218.text: .item() pulls a Python scalar out of an MLX array, which also forces that array to be evaluated. Printing every step would be a hidden synchronization point, which is part of why this only runs every tenth step.

220.text: The same twelve distinct sequence lengths lab 05 hits, since the corpus and the loop are the same. The compile flag is printed alongside so a run with it turned off is self-documenting.

221.text: Steps that paid for a trace, averaged.

222.text: Steps that reused one. The ratio is real but far gentler than JAX's, which is the honest comparison: MLX's compiler is cheaper to invoke, so shape churn hurts less here than it does in lab 05.

227.text: Temperature 0.5 makes generation more conservative: the model favors high-confidence predictions, producing more typical-sounding names.

229.text: Generate 20 brand-new names by sampling from the model's learned distribution.

230.text: Begin each generated name with the beginning-of-sequence token as the initial prompt.

231.text: Generate one character at a time, up to the maximum sequence length. Each step feeds all generated tokens through the full model.

233.text: Run the full model on the current token sequence to predict the next character.

234.text: Grab the logits for the last generated position and divide by temperature. Lower temperature sharpens the distribution toward the top predictions.

235.text: Sample from categorical distribution. MLX's RNG doesn't require explicit key management like JAX.

236.text: When the model outputs the BOS token during generation, it signals the name is complete and we stop adding characters.

238.text: Append the newly sampled token to the growing sequence for the next forward pass.

239.text: Map each token ID back to its character, skipping the leading BOS, to produce the generated name as a readable string.

240.text: Print the finished name. These names were invented by the model from statistical patterns it learned during training.
